I've got one slight complaint so far, and it's that the inventory ui when you're in shops/navigating the convoy feels a little clunky on controller. It doesn't remember your cursor, and whenever you go between the convoy and the like character line up, it forces you to the top character and you have to go down through your unit list again to reach who you want to give items to. Unsure if the same happens on KnM. Will be trying to play on KnM next time I open the game. But otherwise, this is the game that I never knew I needed. I have too many hours across the fire emblem series, and love roguelites too, so the combination is sure to become a new obsession. And the graphics are really charming in a way that I wasn't expecting to like, but immediately kind of fell for :)

高自由度的肉鸽战旗？ 属性成长可预见，通过道具可以转职并且一定程度改变成长； 人物有被动和主动技能，吃书（书学什么可直接预览）、升级ROLL3个随机（可SKIP）； 主动槽有数量限制（最大4，初始不到槽位不到4的可以吃书到4。主动可替换，但会失去被替换的）和无限且可叠加的被动槽； 武器带主动或被动技能，并且没有耐久； 有一个装备槽，可以带坐骑或者防具； 总的来说，各类要素组合下来是真挺好玩的，趣味性十足，有些技能加装备组合会使战斗力大幅提升。 缺点就是暂无自带中文，而且流程相对固定，相对有限的微小随机关卡。

Not recommending it so far, but I'm happy to recommend it if some issues surrounding the roguelite mechanics (or lack thereof) are fixed. [h1]The Bad[/h1] [list] [*]- Map generation sucks. Across numerous maps I was forced to do four encounters in a row without access to stores, class changes, transmutation until I got to the boss of the Act and the give you access to the stores. Even then, these stores are on a linear route, so if you go in without gold you have no ability to sell anything to make more gold to use the vendors. Every vendor should allow selling of surplus crap in your inventory. Also, why the hell are you valuing items at 40 gold but then they sell to the blacksmith for 4 gold? This is idiotic as well. If you're going to value items, they should sell for that value. [*]- Healers where? The only healer I encountered at all was the hero pick Vega with his single target crappy heal that never improved throughout the entire run until I got the general healing upgrade (out of luck on a vendor). Once your healer dies, the run is over. There is no way to self-sustain through encounters without a healer. [*]-Lack of access to class changes. Because you can't access shops readily due to map RNG, you have no access to the ability to buy a class change let alone use one. And even if you get a class change, the odds are you won't have a weapon to use on it. Same goes for mounts. They might exist in game, but if you never see the shops due to your spawn RNG, you never touch the mechanics. [*]-Items - no reliable stores means no potions either or food for out of combat healing. There's also no stronger potions that I found beyond the first level that heals a piddly 18 HP when you've got well over 40 on even your non-tank characters. [*]- Classes - why do classes exist at all when the weapon ability match ups don't match the classes at all? It also doesn't matter when weapon upgrades are so piddling in amount those may as well not exist either. [*]- You can go entire runs without finding weapon upgrades for a relevant class/character. You can also get characters that don't match up at all with whatever you do have in inventory that makes them worthless. This means you hit like a limp noodle in later encounters. [*]- Bugs in encounters where you are forced to do encounters with 20+ enemies in four turns. Once you're over 4 turns, you lose any XP from killing enemies and take damage every turn. You can lose entire encounters worth of XP, loot and characters because of the crappy coding deciding to give you four turns instead of 12. Why isn't there a mode without this turn limit so you can actually play strategically instead of being forced to run screaming to the end goal? This is a SRPG and timed encounters are a gimmick for certain maps, not a mainstay genre feature. I know why it's here, but it's so out of place and crappy for the genre. At the minimum it shouldn't be doing damage every turn. [*]- No meta progression. I'm not a huge fan of the genre to begin with, but roguelite meta progression between runs exists to offset these bad RNG scenarios (like having no stores an entire run). Without it the RNG is especially aggressive in itemisation and there's no impact in doing a run at all unless you unlock a hero through insert arbitrary task here. What this means is that you are entirely at the mercy of RNG. It never gets better because there's no meta progression for it to be better. So you can get four entirely crap runs in a row and why keep playing at that point? You may as well go fire up an actual Fire Emblem game (or Our Adventurer Guild which also does SRPGs right) which doesn't have this problem. [*]- The unknowns - for all I know there are solutions to these issues in the game... but that doesn't matter if I can never access the mechanics in game to see or use them. Is there a revival mechanic? Who knows, I sure as hell never saw it! This is why SRPGs don't limit access to class building and everything else to random nodes a map. [/list] [h1]The Good[/h1] [list] [*]- Accuracy feels on point. If it says 95% hit, it feels like 95% hit, which is a huge part of SRPGs not being total garbage. This felt really good while playing through. [*]- Hero units feel like hero units, but you can also make extremely busted militia characters that are so stacked to the teeth that they may as well be hero units (bow bros reporting in). This allows you to stack a squad together and have them roll through approaching death walls of enemies. I weep for archer not being a dedicated class (that I could find). [*]- Plenty of useful passives not contingent on skill slots, that encourage you moving your characters as a giant death ball block (useful for Act bosses). Plenty of busted skill slot using abilities, but they were harder to find and less useful overall due to scrolls being used to add ability slots being inconsistent. [*]- For the most part, it does feel like Fire Emblem. It has the overall vibe, it has the encounter flow, the actual encounter maps feel similar in layout (but more contained) to how the old school encounters in FE: Awakening worked. I kept expecting to see Awakening's friendship/relationship system to pop up for a combo, but alas it never happened. Maybe they can include something like this is an update. [*] - Difficulty spikes only occurred after what should've been run ending bugs (aforementioned 4 turn map), where if I had the XP from the map as intended it would've been fine. [*] - Good selection of difficulty modes for the masochists among us. [*]-Works on Steam Deck base loadout! This came as a surprise, but apart from a few cutscenes not wanting to work (who cares about that honestly, just skip them or turn them off in settings), for the most part it works. Navigating menus isn't smooth and scrolling up and down your inventory is a nightmare (why does it keep resetting), deployments are a nightmare as well (why can't I deploy from the overall list menu you have a dedicated button for?), but selecting, moving and attack all work fine. The tooltip tool is welcome, but doesn't feel like it was at all designed for controllers. [*] - Robust settings menu to turn off old timey scanline and pixel effects. Bless, give me my ultra sharp anti-aliased, low poly models guys. My eyes are too old and migraines too bad to handle the effects. [*] - Robust settings for increasing combat speed, setting toggles, skipping fluff and getting straight to the action. Very welcome. [*] - Basically, everything that's not the roguelite mechanics works great. The more exposed you become to the roguelite mechanics, the worse the game feels. I really wish they'd just made this without the gimmicks and released it as a proper FE style clone. [/list] This should have been an Early Access game. It has redeeming features in the actual combat, but the implementation of the "roguelite" mechanics are total garbage. Devs, please release a version or mode where we just have universal access to stores, because right now, not having consistent or reliable access to shops per chapter makes most of the game's systems irrelevant. I hope you guys all liked playing Impossible Scenarios in Starcraft 1 back in the day, because that's what this game is with the current design decisions. If this was releases as a straight SRPG/FE clone it would've been a far superior experience than them now having to balance crappy roguelite systems. It's still fun, but how do you recommend a roguelite that has no meta progression to offset the RNG?

[h2] Solid game with some frustrations [/h2] This is a pretty good game if you're hankering for a shorter tactics game with replayability. My first fully completed run clocked in at about 5 hours, Although I did play out the maps as the dialogue was being played out because it was repeat dialogue (Repeat dialogue can be set to not interrupt your gameplay). In combat if your main leader's hp drops to 0 your run will immediately fail, if any other character drops to 0 they will be in a downed state which will allow you to save them for the rest of the run (No turn limit on the downed state, but beware of the overall turn limit of the combat encounters). In the overworld you'll find combat encounters, physical weapon shop, magical weapon shop, sub-class shop, treasure chests and campfires. in the shops you'll be able to purchase: [list] [*]Weapons (which each come with their own in-built ability) [*]Memories (Roguelike relics that buff your team) [*]Sub-classes (which will add additional stats and increase/decreease growths depending on the choice and unlock the abilities from that class to be learned by your character) [*]Mounts (Horses/Flying Mounts). The mounts are included the weapon strengths/weaknesses chart but do not determine what class you are like in Fire Emblem, they are treated as equipment with stats and can be given to anyone in your party. [/list] While I'm enjoying the freedom of the overworld I'm not entirely sure how I feel about it's implementation in regards to the time limit forced upon you. There's a 'time limit' of 4 combat encounters until you are forced to beat the boss encounter for that act. Meaning you kind of want to max out on non-combat encounters on whatever map gets generated for you. If you do not plan accordingly to be as close to the center as possible after your 4th combat encounter you'll have to travel from node to node to get to the boss encounters, receiving debuffs/general negative effects as you travel. So overall while I am honestly really enjoying this game because I'm really enjoying the difficulty, there are systems in place that kind of put a damper on things. But if you're someone that really enjoys playing tactics games I can definitely recommend it. Note: [u] This is a roguelike, not necessarily a roguelite. [/u] There's no real power progression outside of your runs. No additional relics, weapons or the like unlock from what I can tell. You can however unlock new leaders (main characters for the run) and difficulty by beating the highest difficulty available to you. Outside of that, Things you've encountered during your runs will be recorded in a codex in the main menu. Hope this review gave you some information you were looking for

I want to like this game. I want it to be good. I believe it CAN be good. It's just not there yet. My biggest criticism would be that this feels like game that just came into early access rather than a full release. It has a pretty decent foundation but boy oh boy, it really lacks in content, UI clarification & design, and replay value. First run of the game and I already had over half of the codex unlocked. There are a very limited number of classes, most of which honestly blend together, and the skill pool is equally shallow. This makes it incredibly easy and consistent to get multiple units that juggernaut their way through the game. The difficulty is a complete joke. I'm 30 hours in, picking the highest difficulty available to me every run, and not once have I felt threatened. I don't even check stats. I rush in regardless of how many enemies there are and I'm never punished for it. There's no effective weaponry and crits are reduced to x1.5 damage I believe so there's no danger whatsoever. And mounts. Oh boy are mounts overpowered. Free stats, large movement, no counterplay. Just a pathetic +1 damage +10% hit from ritual mages who barely tickle. Big deal. Standard maps have a fair amount of variety which is nice but the boss maps are static. Gets old REAL quick. The economy even on the lowest difficulty is a joke. Shops are borderline useless without specific memories (think of them like relics from games like StS) that make them affordable. There are random drops of course, but items only sell for 10% value. You're more than likely only visiting a shop once or twice per run unless you randomly got a pickpocket skill / yoink spell to get gold from enemies. Not that you NEED the shop, as I said the game is incredibly easy even without ever buying anything, but I feel like this is bad design that punishes casual players incredibly hard. Instead it is far more efficient to dump everything you aren't using into the alchemist and just working with whatever you're given. I think one of the biggest disappointments is that the recruited militia units are all pre-generated. You'll see the same faces every run because there's only roughly fourteen of them in the pool. Where's the fun in that? I can handle the lords being static since we have all run to craft them the way we want, but the recruits units should be more random! Even if it means getting worse units overall, any fire emblem vet can tell you that making a bad unit into a god is one of the most enjoyable experiences in the genre. A roguelite game is the perfect platform to play with this, but unfortunately the sandbox that we've been given to play with is rather limited. All-in-all, would I recommend this game? No. Not right now. Keep an eye on it if you are interested to see what kind of updates happen in the future. As I mentioned before, I think it has the potential to be really good, it just has a ways to go to get there.
Recommended for Fire Emblem fans, good for the price, excited to see what the devs will add

Yeah, it's good. A lot of modern Fire Emblems have pulled towards rewinds and survivability, but Astral Throne just fully leans into the lethality. You'll miss treasures and units on missions and you won't reload. Your units will get KO'd and you'll have to decide whether to pick them back up or push on to finish the mission. Everything's on a turn timer, and enemies are spamming in constantly, and it's the same old RNG you remember. It's challenging, and the game expects you to fail, and this is freeing. Astral Throne is not a Fire Emblem you need to play perfectly. It has a story, that story is very character centric, and you can see different sides of the story based on which starting lords you choose, but that story is also completely secondary to the fun of trying to clear stages with the tools you have. Sometimes life gives you an unusuable level 2 mage and you have to make unuseable level 2 mage lemonade. Within this context, Astral Throne is a lot of fun. I personally prefer the storytelling and custom map design of more traditional Fire Emblems, but there's a verve to Astral Throne that is hard to deny. Sometimes it's fun to just be good at a genre, and to let the consequences of your choices ride. Edit: Some small quibbles. The item interface takes a little getting used to. Often, if you go into the caravan screen during the main map, the camera will pivot and send you flying out into the ocean. The doctor feels NECESSARY due to the scarcity of healing otherwise, which the game is constructed around. This makes it so that seeing how characters other than the doctor interact with each other is kinda discouraged, which undercuts the care that went into writing so many different unique interactions. Even with the doctor, the game isn't easy, even on easy---I think some of the other classes could get minor healing abilities without it neutralizing the doctor's role in the meta or trivializing game difficulty. 2nd Edit: I'm an idiot. Foci have healing abilities. The middle mouse to lock window to read text system is awkward, so I've been mostly not reading abilities, but lol I cannot do that and expect to play well. 3rd Edit: This really does fix all of the issues I've had with Shadow Dragon, Geneology, and Thracia. It's amazing how such a small nudge to the design priorities of a game can set to rights the whole play experience. Shozou Kaga's design is super punishing in a traditional campaign structure, but in a roguelike? Where you can lose and still win? You have a lot more freedom to experiment and improve and adapt to changing conditions because you're not having to savescum to pass chapters---and in turn, the game can be a little more forgiving because you're not constantly reloading to optimize stat growth and playing with three walkthroughs to make sure you don't miss a recruitable with byzantine recruit conditions. 4th Edit: I do think the final boss is perhaps a bit overtuned, and requires you to have fully read his entire stat sheet before approaching him or else the map is now unwinnable. Highkey, great final boss fight for a non-roguelike fire emblem. The timer and need to hunt the captains adds pressure without necessarily making the boss' stats big. Except the boss' stats are also big and his range is gigantic so if you aggroed him before taking out the captains you just lose. The length of a given run does not make me want to replay the game to fight him again, and the extreme lack of unlocks does not make me want to tinker too much with different builds. I do think Astral Throne is worth it overall, and nails most of the risks it takes. The spots where it's shaky are minor blemishes compared with the rest of the design.

Edit: The final boss is such a slap to the face. I'm changing this to a not recommend, the final boss being the straw that broke the camel's back. [spoiler]First, you normally fight about 1-3 enemy elites in previous battles. The battle before the final boss, there was 5 elites + 1 boss. Sure it was hard but still doable and the elites can be mostly skipped as long as you get the boss. In the final boss, you face off with 10 elites of which all directly buff the boss if left undealt with. Second, the final boss has an RNG gimmick which involves weapon type advantages. So basically the boss draws 5 random weapons every turn. If you get unlucky and he draws weapons that counter your character, that means you pretty much can't do any damage that turn. If you're unlucky and he draws a weapon you're either weak or neutral against, then you would be doing basically 0 damage, maybe 1-3 damage if you're lucky. The boss has 305hp. This was on the beginner difficulty too. On the other hand, the boss will usually deal about 70% of your hp on average when he fights back, lethal if you're weak to it. If you're lucky however, you would think you could deal some damage. Nope. To put into perspective, i had my leader with several buffs, skill usage, weapon advantage and equal level to the boss deal a whopping 30 damage in total. This means to kill the boss you'd need to get lucky about 10 times. This is also a DPS leader so for the militia/recruits you can expect about half the amount of damage assuming the same criteria above. Even while playing my absolute best of my abilities and having to adapt to the unknown gimmicks and such, i only barely manage to hit the boss to 30hp left before he started regenerating everything back because i hit the time limit. Honestly feels like a waste of my 8 hours just to end up facing something that you'd need prior knowledge to be able to beat. So to sum it up, when you fight this boss you have only 20 rounds to finish the fight. So in 20 rounds, you are expected to: [list] [*] Traverse about 50 tiles of which most units average 5 move per turn [*] Defeat at least 5/10 of the elites, most which do not spawn until later in the game + are scattered across the map [*] Go out of your way to open up the boss room via keys/doors and mechanic barriers [*] Wait 1 turn for the boss to "wake up" when you enter his room [*] Deal with the boss' weapon roulette gimmick where you can only damage him on some turns [*] All the while dealing with the onslaught of enemies that keep's coming [/list][/spoiler] Some other gripes about the game: [list] [*] The UI/UX needs more polish, especially in the shops/caravan part. Certain navigation/interactions are very tedious to perform. [*] Controller support is mostly useable but there are some key parts that is either hard or impossible to navigate on a controller so a M/KB is needed [*] It is way too easy to misclick the "Wait/End turn" button which essentially forgos that unit's turn (And with how important each move is, this is a very costly mistake) [*] The unlockables in the game are staggeringly non-existant; Pretty much just 5 new heroes and difficulty levels. It's probably more accurate to call this a procedural generated arcade rather than a a rogue-lite. [*] There is too much RNG involved in this game. The recruits you get are completely random so you just need to wing it. On top of that you need to train said recruits but the game pretty much offers no chances to actually train them + punishes you and forces you to progress quickly. [*] In line with the above, the game kind of encourages you to "optimize" your battle time considering how rushed you are. This means you would purposely stall winning a battle simply for your characters to grind some exp for levels by doing arbitrary stuff like healing each other or lightly damaging an enemy. [/list] A great example of a roguelite that is hard [b][i]but fair[/i][/b] is Binding of Isaac. You are able to pretty much win the game and beat mother even on your first run given you play very well. Later gameplay slowly becomes harder as newer enemies and bosses appear but also gives more variety via items, characters and skills thereby giving you even better fighting chance. This game on the other hand is just hard [b][i]and unfair[/i][/b]... Original review below: Very well done tactics type rougelite with an emphasis on technically disposable militias. (Fire Emblem / FF Tactics) The overall game is really good; You are always outnumbered and outgunned but with proper planning and tactics you can usually incur very minimal losses. In the event you either miscalculate or get unlucky, you'd need to replan your tactics on whether to keep going forward to minimize your damage. Very well done risk-reward type of thing here. The loses here are also no joke; Death of your caravan crew is permanent unless you rescue them so there is always that lingering worry that will keep you from sending someone on a suicide mission. Hopefully the devs lean in more into this permadeath aspect as this makes the game a lot more unique/interesting as opposed to having death being inconsiquential. Im really in awe at the hero interactions in this game that adds lots of personality to the character and the game itself. There are also plenty of unlockable characters so you can definitely mix and match them to hear their unique voice lines guided towards various different backgrounds. My only gripe so far is the management of inventory in items using a controller, specifically the lack of any quick move button. Having to select/pick an item from a character then navigate to/from the caravan (Main inventory) just to scroll all the way down to an empty space is really tedious when having to do so often.

这是我目前为止玩到的第一款rogue与战旗完美结合的游戏。 游戏总共三张地图，每张地图都有商店、宝箱、战斗地点、竞技场等。前两张地图都有四场常规战，一场boss战，第三个地图是最终boss战，所以总共11个战斗场景，一次通关十几小时。 每场战斗存在回合限制，超过回合限制可以继续战斗，但不会获得战斗经验，而且会受到扣血惩罚，所以每场战斗需要合理规划，速战速决。 游戏开始可以选择两个英雄，一个领队，一个副手，每次常规战可以招募战场中的随机民兵队友，到达第二张地图可以再次选择一个英雄。 职业可分为民兵职业和英雄职业，民兵职业有战士、骑士、侦察兵、魔法师、僧侣、德鲁伊和学者，英雄职业有医生、十字军、战斗魔法师、飞骑、傀儡师等。 技能分为职业技能、武器技能、属性技能、支援技能和通用技能。 每个角色最多4个技能槽，游戏开始领队4个技能槽，副手3个技能槽，民兵2-3个技能槽，简单技能不占用技能槽。队友每次升级可以从随机3个技能中选择学习1个技能。 武器间存在克制关系。物理武器分为轻武器、盾武器、重武器、远程武器，魔法武器分为：动物魔法、元素魔法、物质魔法、仪式魔法。 每个职业都有对应的可学习的武器类型列表，但招募到的角色一开始学习到的武器类型是随机的，角色武器列表置亮的图标表示已学习的武器类型，置灰的图标表示尚未学习的武器类型，需要从武器技能书中随机习得；对于不可学习的武器类型，也可以从专门的武器技能书中随机习得。 商店可以购买坐骑、物理武器、魔法武器、技能书等。游戏金钱还是比较紧张的，但看到好装备就不要犹豫，当然需要在玩过几轮后才知道哪些装备是看到必入的。 游戏的战斗场景以及人物建模看起来稍显粗糙，我在入手前也是有过犹豫的，但入手体验后还是觉得挺香的，我认为是款优秀的rogue策略游戏，值得不同主角多周目游玩体验以及更高难度下的挑战，在每轮队友、技能和武器的不同组合下，每次游玩都有不一样的体验。

Astral Throne does a great job blending the SRPG and roguelike genres. I'm writing this review mainly as an SRPG player who doesn't have a ton of time to commit to long campaigns anymore. As an SRPG player, you'll want to give Astral Throne a shot if you enjoy: - Highly customizable characters, e.g. skills, weapons, mounts, skills, subclasses - Minimal but meaningful preparation between chapters - Replayability; no two runs are the same and you will need to adapt to the RNG - Low overhead; no hub world - Low commitment; max 11 chapters per campaign - Low-moderate unit count, 4-10 deployment slots You may want to skip this one if you want: - An incredibly engaging story - Lengthy conversations between cast members - Minigames between chapters In terms of difficulty, I'd place Astral Throne somewhere around FE Fates Conquest hard/classic. Not too bad once you get used to the mechanics but there's definitely a learning curve.

I don't really like the game despite having finished every FE game in existence on hardest difficulty. The graphics are just...yeah I hate them, so the good part had to come from the gameplay entirely. However, the battles become increasingly obnoxious in the second half of the run, especially once you start playing on difficulties which add more evasion to all enemies. This is my biggest gripe with the game...the displayed hit % feels incredibly off. I lost on the final boss on first run because he managed to land a crit on Cetus with 5% to even hit, nvm crit. Not to mention 85% chance to hits are below 50% in actuality while below 50% chance to hit is, well...don't even bother, you'll maybe land 1 out of 10 attempts while the reverse is of course true for when the enemy has this kind of hit chance. There are also precious few ways to increase your hit chance. Instead, the game gives you weapons that decrease your hit chance (e.g. bardiche) and it even has a character unlock requirement based on landing a hit at below 10% hit chance (haha, yeah, good 'luck' with that one, you might get it after 10000 attempts). Plus, weapon advantage barely matters in the increased hit rate sense, whereas on Fire Emblem it would matter to the point that you could mitigate hit % 'bad luck' to a minimum. But especially this being a roguelike makes this hit chance issue a cardinal sin for the potential enjoyment of the game. Builds are useless when only 1 or 2 of your 8+ characters are able to land hits on enemies while the map expects you to split your group across several corners of the map. Furthermore, in the latest run, on the book burning stage, the blood caster girl decides to just leave *after* you start the map, completely scuffing the planned strategy beforehand and I ended up losing because of it (and not enough characters being able to land their hits). And that is what caused me to ultimately write this negative review. My entire time playing this game has felt like a waste of time strategically, and the only bit of joy I got out of it was from the interactions at the start of a map between the lead characters. In conclusion, only buy this if you're ok with sticking to the difficulties which do not raise enemy evasion and if you don't mind \negative/ eye candy graphics, doing re-runs with your randomly decided DEI flavored character designs (the only flavor) that you'll be able to recruit. Or if you're a masochist who just wants to feel pain constantly while trying to unlock 'harder' difficulty modes; you'll definitely find that here in spades.

Really fun Fire Emblem-like roguelite. It can use some balance updates, but it's still great in it's current state. Now, I do recommend this game, but it's not nearly as replayable compared to other roguelites. I'm not saying that you can only play it once, but that it will get old within 5-15 playthroughs. This is because once you have figured out a map, your moves for that map will be similar across all playthroughs. You won't encounter each map on each playthrough (aside from the 3 "boss" maps), but you encounter them often enough that it gets old fast. I don't think this is a fault of the game, it's just the nature of how a game like this plays out. If they tripled the number of boss maps and doubled the number or standard maps, it would go a long way towards increasing the replayability. Still, I think most will get 20-40 hours of enjoyment out of this game, so I would recommend it. I certainly had a blast playing it and I'll probably revisit it in a year when I've forgotten what all the maps look like.

This game is so close to being something special, but held back by decisions that limit play too much imo. You get approximately 4 fights before you're forced into the final segment. Less if you don't clear the stages fast enough. This means your characters will probably be around lvl 10 going into the endgame due to exp scaling. And after a certain level, your units feel like they just stop getting exp altogether until you move on to the next chapter...which also mean their fights waste exp... Though with the SHEER ENEMY DENSITY, maybe that doesn't matter too much. The limited number of fights also means you have a limited amount of gold/exp to farm before progressing. This is made worse by the fact that the few items you DO get will only sell at 10% of their cost. You may as well just destroy items you don't want or just gamble them in the transmute pools. Speaking of which, I'm not sure if blue items are the highest rarity, but I didn't encounter anything higher. Even then if it's one you can't use, you can MAYBE afford a potion by selling it or pray you get a unit/book that makes use of it, lol. Finally, despite the punishing limitations, the game was actually enjoyable as units' builds and skills slowly add up and everything starts to click...until around the final 3 fights of the run. As soon as you see teleportation panels, the game just becomes incredibly unfun. Not only are they not intuitive on which ones connect to where (despite color matching, they don't all connect with all spots of the same color), but the enemies somehow SPIKE in difficulty beyond what you can bring at this stage. I said you hit around lvl 10-ish with your units by endgame...and the enemies feel like lvl 15 or lvl 20...and they VASTLY outnumber you. Don't even get me STARTED on the final boss. Giant crystal with 300 HP and 40 Defense and Resistance, 5 max-rarity weapons only it can use (of all ranges), and constant self-buffing and a self-heal for 30 damage. You'll be LUCKY to get 3-8 damage in at the cost of an entire unit's HP (because it also hits like a truck), only for it to heal it all back and smack 3 of your units at once. This, in addition to the swarm of enemies constantly pouring in behind you and I don't see how the final boss is actually winnable on any difficulty. MAYBE if you invest all your units into party/proximity buffs into a single stat (all-physical or all-magic) and pray you can buff hard enough, but...idk. Anyway, super-long rant over. tl;dr Would I recommend this game? Tbh, only for Fire Emblem masochists that want to add a roguelike element to what's the closest thing to a randomizer kaizo you can get. I rate it a 30-strength "All Attacks have +5 Range" Axe-Knight on a fort out of 10.

I'm really mixed on Astral Throne. I really wanted to like this more. I don't think I'd outright recommend it, but I wouldn't warn others to stay away either. The scope of Astral Throne is impressive and ambitious. I really dig the art style and animations. The gameplay is heavily inspired by Fire Emblem and Final Fantasy Tactics. The game pulls off those elements really well here, though I wish the upgrades were more impactful. The main element holding this game back for me is actually the roguelike mechanics. Because each run takes so long (at least 3 to 4 hours), I don't feel compelled to start another run. I wonder if this game would have benefitted more from a longer campaign and dropping the roguelike parts. Unfortunately, the game is also pretty buggy, particularly the UI.

I'd be lying if I said this was my favorite roguelite, but it's definitely a good time. The character and team building are quite deep, and the game really encourages you to lean into broken synergies. The campaign doesn't feel like it has much variety, but that really isn't a problem for me when my approach to the battles is wildly different each run. If there's anything I haven't enjoyed, it's probably that when every unit has an ability, you should be using those on every spare turn to grind exp, which gets quite tedious (think grinding clerics in Fire Emblem, but for every character); there's a time limit on battles, so this isn't that big a deal, though. Some of the later maps have considerable performance issues, too, with my 6 year-old laptop struggling to hit 20fps on the second to last map, but this didn't bother me much, what with the game being turn-based. Overall, it's a very easy recommend to anyone who likes both roguelites and SRPGs.

I'm also kind of disappointed that rather than iterating on and fixing this game, they're announcing a sequel.

If you’re a tactical RPG fanatic, like me, then I would absolutely recommend Astral Throne. From the first battle, it’s clear this game understands what makes the genre special. The combat is tight, deliberate, and deeply strategic without ever feeling bloated. Every move matters. Positioning, unit synergy, and ability timing all play meaningful roles, and the difficulty hits that sweet spot where you’re constantly thinking but rarely frustrated. When you win, it feels earned. The class and progression systems are where Astral Throne really shines. There’s a ton of room to experiment, and builds feel impactful rather than cosmetic. Units evolve in ways that meaningfully change your tactical options, which keeps the gameplay fresh even dozens of hours in. It scratches that classic Fire Emblem / FFT itch while still carving out its own identity. Performance-wise, it runs smoothly and feels polished. No jank, no weird pacing issues, just a well crafted tactical experience that respects your time. If you love tactical RPGs with meaningful strategy, strong build variety, and a clear creative vision, Astral Throne is absolutely worth your time. One of the most satisfying indie strategy experiences I’ve played.

Booted it up, played it, beat it on my first run after about eight and a half hours. Though probably an hour or two of that time was due to getting distracted during the run. 1. The Camera during battle is a pain in the ass. Switching to watch the attacks play out anytime you're near a way is going to have you planting against the floor instead of actually watching the action. 2. The Bosses are cheap, especially the final boss. If the difficulty of your game comes from hyper-inflated stats and enemies completely breaking the rules of combat (no counters, AoEs, etc), maybe rethink how you're designing your fights. 3. There's really not much "story" involved or any information presented to the player. Its thin enough that I couldn't spread it satisfyingly on a cracker. You get some very mild changes in dialogue depending on who is in your party; however, none of it actually changes the story. The only thing that can possibly change is the three paragraph text scroll you get at the end of the game for your party lead. 4. It's short and the difficulty is wildly inconsistent. Some fights you just breeze through, others, especially the final fight are mind-numbing in how unbalanced they are. 5. The Time-limits on the fights are arbitrary and don't actually reinforce tactical play. Just make you overly focus on damage output, and nothing else. Which would be fine, if the game didn't also kick you in the teeth with enemies with startlingly high evasion and defenses that negate almost all damage. Long story-short. Don't waste your time on this one. The game is rudimentary and aside from a first run, there's nothing compelling enough about it to engage with beyond curiosity. Its a game that promises the moon, but only manages to hand over a rock.
